blocks.value: Even experienced investors make mistakes. The aim is not to predict every market move or avoid every error; it is to recognise avoidable mistakes before they cause serious damage. Many costly decisions happen when people rush, ignore risk or rely on incomplete information.
01. Investing without research — Buying without understanding what the business does or how it makes money.
02. Overconcentration — Putting too much money into one company or sector, so one setback can hurt a large part of the portfolio.
03. Following rumours — Treating social media tips or unverified claims as a substitute for independent research.
04. Chasing rising prices — Buying mainly because a share is going up and fearing that you will miss out (FOMO).
05. Panic selling — Selling during a fall without checking whether the business or your original investment reason has actually changed.
06. Ignoring fundamentals — Overlooking important information such as debt, cash flow, profitability or valuation.
07. Trading without a plan — Entering a trade without deciding in advance what would make you exit or how much risk you are taking.
08. Risking essential money — Investing money needed for rent, fees, medical needs or other near-term expenses.

Imagine This: Driving without knowing your destination or checking the route can lead to wrong turns. Investing without understanding why you bought something can create the same problem. When the price changes, you have no clear basis for deciding whether to hold, sell or review the investment.

One common mistake is confusing a good company with a good investment at any price. A business may have strong products and growing profits, but its share price may already reflect very high expectations. Valuation matters because the price you pay affects the return you may earn.

An investor buys a share because a friend recommends it. They do not check what the company does, its debt or why the price has risen. A few weeks later, the share falls sharply after disappointing results. The investor sells in panic because there was no original research or plan to guide the decision.

Another mistake is confusing a temporary price fall with a permanent business problem—or assuming every fall is temporary. The correct response depends on evidence. Review company announcements, financial results and the original reason for investing rather than relying only on the chart or a message from someone else.

Before investing, explain in your own words what you are buying, why it belongs in your portfolio, what could go wrong and how much you can afford to allocate. If you cannot answer these questions, pause and learn more.

Avoid borrowing money to invest in volatile assets or using money needed for rent, fees, medical needs or other essential expenses. A market loss can become much more damaging when it creates debt or affects day-to-day needs.

blocks.question: Which is a common investing mistake?
Why can buying only because a share price is rising be risky?
choices: A rising price guarantees more gains
The decision may be driven by FOMO rather than research

blocks.question: Can a good company be a poor investment at an excessive price?
choices: Yes, the price paid affects potential returns
Only if it is a small company

blocks.question: What should an investor do when a share falls?
choices: Review the facts and the original investment reason

blocks.question: Why should essential-expense money not be put into volatile investments?
choices: A loss could affect important near-term needs
